speaker: Doctor
text: Can you describe what the dizziness feels like to you, and does it seem to be triggered by moving your head? Have you experienced any hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or a feeling of fullness in your ear?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text: Do these episodes of spinning last for seconds or minutes, and do you experience nausea or vomiting when they occur? Can you also confirm if turning over in bed or looking up specifically triggers these spells?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis.

speaker: Doctor
text: The brief, position-triggered spinning episodes strongly suggest Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo, but I need to confirm if you have ever experienced fainting or chest pain during these spells. Also, have you noticed any new weakness or numbness on one side of your face or body?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical or surgical history. No history of Meniere's disease, vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis. Social history: Retired school teacher. Lives alone. Non-smoker, occasional wine. Enjoys light gardening.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any fainting, chest pain, or one-sided weakness during these spells? Also, have you noticed any new ringing in your ears or a feeling of fullness? REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Vital Signs: Temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), Blood Pressure 130/85 mmHg, Heart Rate 77 bpm, Respiratory Rate 14 breaths/min. Neurological Examination: Cranial nerves normal, coordination normal (no ataxia or dysmetria), gait steady (no imbalance outside of vertigo episodes). Dix-Hallpike Maneuver: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). Audiometry: Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss consistent with presbycusis; no sudden hearing drops. Videonystagmography: Normal vestibular response except for the response elicited during the Dix-Hallpike maneuver (consistent with BPPV). MRI Brain: No evidence of central lesions or infarcts.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver showing right-sided horizontal nystagmus and normal imaging, the diagnosis is clear. DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) affecting the right ear.
